scope: Ranks 251–1500, resolved current similar-word teaching and typed recall. Includes retained baseline cards; do not infer no synonyms from unchanged status.
grading: Only exact headword/explicit alternatives pass after case/edge-punctuation normalization. Accent/spelling slips and recognized inflections get score-free correction opportunities, not immediate rejection. Dictionary-form recall is explicit. Cloze and recognition acceptance are separate. Broad main teaching examples may show a different legitimate sense from selected typed cue; classify teaching alignment separately from false facts.

sections.title: To finish
sections.text: Terminar, acabar and concluir overlap for finishing an activity. Acabar de + infinitive also describes something just done; that construction is different.

sections.title: To use
sections.text: Usar, utilizar and emplear all work for using a tool. Emplear also means employ a person; that extra sense is not shared by all three.

sections.title: To happen
sections.text: Ocurrir, suceder and pasar overlap for events happening. Pasar has many other senses, including passing and spending time.

sections.title: Different
sections.text: Diferente and distinto overlap for things that are not the same. Distinto can also emphasize distinctness; neither requires total opposition.

sections.title: To answer
sections.text: Responder and contestar overlap when answering a question. Responder de means answer for or take responsibility for something.

sections.title: To need
sections.text: Necesitar and requerir overlap in the sense of needing. Requerir can also mean formally request or demand; these additional uses are not interchangeable in every sentence.

sections.title: To provide
sections.text: Proporcionar and brindar can mean provide help. Ofrecer can merely offer it, without its being received, so the offer and provision senses need to be kept apart.

sections.title: To continue
sections.text: Continuar and seguir overlap for continuing an activity. Seguir also means follow; that sense is separate.

sections.title: To obtain
sections.text: Obtener, conseguir and lograr overlap for obtaining a result. Conseguir and lograr also take an infinitive directly for managing to do something; obtener does not.

sections.title: To start
sections.text: Iniciar, empezar and comenzar can start an activity expressed as a noun. Empezar and comenzar use a before an infinitive; iniciar does not replace them in that pattern.

sections.title: To remove
sections.text: Quitar and retirar overlap for removing something. Sacar specifically suggests taking it out of somewhere; not every removal has that direction.
examples: Retira el vaso de la mesa.
Remove the glass from the table.

sections.title: To include
sections.text: Incluir, incorporar, agregar, añadir and sumar all fit adding a name to a list. Integrar emphasizes bringing parts into a whole; integration can involve more than listing something as included.
examples: Incluye su nombre en la lista.
Include his name on the list.

sections.title: To indicate
sections.text: Señalar and indicar can both point out a location. Señalar can involve a gesture or marking; indicar can also give instructions.
examples: Indica el lugar en el mapa.
Indicate the place on the map.

sections.title: To guarantee
sections.text: Garantizar and asegurar overlap in giving assurance. Asegurar also means secure physically or insure; those uses require their own context.

sections.title: To state
sections.text: Afirmar emphasizes asserting truth. Declarar can be a statement, especially a formal one; a declaration need not be a claim of certainty.
examples: She states that it is true.

sections.title: To assert
sections.text: Afirmar asserts something as true. Declarar can also state it, often formally; it does not always imply certainty.

sections.title: To declare
sections.text: Declarar can make a statement; afirmar asserts. Declarar also has special uses such as declaring income or declaring love.

sections.title: To transform
sections.text: Transformar expresses a change of form or nature. Cambiar is broader: a change need not amount to a transformation.
examples: Transforma el edificio en un museo.
She transforms the building into a museum.

sections.title: To change
sections.text: Cambiar, alterar and modificar overlap in changing an arrangement. Transformar implies a change in form or nature, which may be more substantial.

sections.title: To constitute
sections.text: Formar, constituir and conformar overlap when parts make up a whole. Conformarse con means settle for; it is a different construction.
examples: Three people make up the team.

sections.title: To help
sections.text: Ayudar and auxiliar overlap in helping someone. Auxiliar often appears in assistance or rescue contexts; ayudar is the general everyday verb.

sections.title: To win
sections.text: Ganar and vencer overlap for being victorious. Ganar also means earn money; vencer can take the defeated opponent directly.

sections.title: To inform
sections.text: Informar a alguien de algo and comunicar algo a alguien both convey information, with different object patterns. Comunicar also covers communication more broadly.

sections.title: To reveal
sections.text: Revelar means make hidden information known. Descubrir can mean uncover it or discover it for oneself; learning a fact and announcing it are different events.

sections.title: To try
sections.text: Intentar takes an infinitive directly. Tratar de + infinitive also means try to; probar can mean test, taste or try something out.
examples: She tries to open the door.

sections.title: End
sections.text: Fin and final overlap for an ending. Término can also mean end, while conclusión may be a conclusion reached by reasoning; those broader senses need context.
examples: El final de la película es triste.
The end of the film is sad.

sections.title: Beginning
sections.text: Principio, inicio and comienzo overlap for a beginning. Principio also means a principle; that ethical or theoretical sense is separate.
examples: El inicio del curso es mañana.

sections.title: Result
sections.text: Resultado, consecuencia and efecto overlap for outcomes of actions. Resultado also names a score, and efecto has scientific and legal uses that need their own context.
examples: Fue una consecuencia de la decisión.
It was a consequence of the decision.

sections.title: Reason
sections.text: Motivo and razón overlap for a reason to act. Causa names what produces an effect, which need not be someone's conscious motive.
examples: Explica el motivo de su decisión.
She explains the reason for her decision.

sections.title: Goal
sections.text: Objetivo and meta overlap for an aim. Propósito also names an intention; the intended purpose and a measurable target need not be identical.

sections.title: Concept
sections.text: Concepto is a concept or notion. Idea is broader and can be a proposal or thought, so not every idea is a defined concept.

sections.title: Name
sections.text: Nombre and denominación overlap for the name of something. Denominación often concerns a designation or category; nombre is also a person's name.
examples: I do not remember the name.

sections.title: Area
sections.text: Zona, área and región overlap for geographical areas. Región often suggests a larger or recognized territory; área also names a surface measurement.

sections.title: Route
sections.text: Camino, ruta and vía overlap as ways of reaching a destination. Camino can be a physical path; vía can also be a means or railway track.

sections.title: Way
sections.text: Modo, manera and forma overlap for a way of doing something. Forma also describes shape; modo has grammatical uses.

sections.title: Power
sections.text: Poder names power or authority. Fuerza is force or strength; it may contribute to power but is not the same as legal authority.
examples: She has the power to decide.

sections.title: Price
sections.text: Precio is the selling price. Costo/coste is a cost, and valor is value or worth; these amounts can differ.

sections.title: Ability
sections.text: Capacidad and habilidad overlap for ability. Habilidad often emphasizes skill, while capacidad can also be capacity or potential.
examples: She has a skill for drawing.

sections.title: Illness
sections.text: Enfermedad and dolencia overlap for illness. Dolencia can also describe an ailment or complaint without naming a specific disease.

sections.title: Company
sections.text: Compañía and empresa overlap for a company. Negocio is a business or commercial activity and can also mean a deal; compañía also means companionship.
examples: She works at a small company.

sections.title: Act
sections.text: Acto and acción overlap for an act. Hecho can name a deed but also a fact or event, whether or not someone deliberately did it.
examples: It was an act of generosity.

sections.title: Piece of information
sections.text: Dato is an individual item of information. Información is usually the information as a whole; datos is the plural corresponding to data.
examples: One piece of information is missing.

sections.title: Answer
sections.text: Respuesta and contestación overlap for a reply. Respuesta can also describe a reaction to an event rather than a verbal answer.
examples: I am waiting for your answer.

sections.title: Film
sections.text: Película and filme overlap for a film. Película also means a thin layer, so that physical meaning needs separate treatment.

sections.title: Face
sections.text: Cara and rostro overlap for a face. Rostro can sound more formal or literary; cara also means a side or surface.

sections.title: Ground
sections.text: Suelo, tierra and terreno overlap in ground-related senses. Tierra can mean soil or land; terreno emphasizes a tract or type of land, and suelo also means a floor. Both tierra and suelo fit the selected soil cue: earth that supports plant growth.

sections.title: Boy
sections.text: Chico and muchacho overlap for a boy or young person. Niño specifically suggests a child; the applicable age range depends on context.

sections.title: Opportunity
sections.text: Ocasión and oportunidad overlap for a chance. Ocasión can also mean an occasion or time when something happens, without implying a favorable opportunity.

sections.title: Danger
sections.text: Peligro emphasizes danger; riesgo often emphasizes the possibility or exposure to harm. They overlap in ordinary speech but are distinguished in technical contexts. Both are accepted for these ordinary-language cues; no technical distinction is specified.
examples: There is a danger of fire.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Conclusión can be a reasoned conclusion or an ending. Fin names an end or purpose, not a reasoned judgment.

sections.title: Near
sections.text: Próximo and cercano overlap for spatial nearness. Próximo also means next; cercano does not replace it in every future-time expression.

sections.title: Next
sections.text: Siguiente and próximo overlap for what comes next. Próximo also means near; siguiente always involves a sequence.
examples: La próxima reunión es el lunes.
The next meeting is on Monday.

sections.title: Previous
sections.text: Anterior and previo overlap for something earlier. Anterior also describes a position at the front in anatomical or spatial uses.

sections.title: Current
sections.text: Actual and presente overlap for current. Actual does not normally mean actual in the English sense of real; presente also means present rather than absent.

sections.title: Real
sections.text: Real and verdadero overlap for genuine or real. Verdadero also means true rather than false; real can also mean royal.

sections.title: Obvious
sections.text: Claro, evidente and obvio overlap for something obvious. Claro also means clear, pale or light; those senses are distinct.

sections.title: Difficult
sections.text: Difícil and complicado overlap for something hard to do. Complicado can specifically mean complex, so not every difficult task is complicated.

sections.title: Main
sections.text: Principal and primordial overlap for primary importance. Principal can also name the main item in an arrangement, not necessarily something fundamental in origin.

sections.title: Global
sections.text: Mundial and global overlap for worldwide scope. Global can also mean overall, considering something as a whole rather than worldwide.

sections.title: Safe
sections.text: Seguro can mean safe or secure. Protegido means protected; protection is a means of safety, not a guarantee of it. Seguro also means certain.

sections.title: Strong
sections.text: Fuerte and intenso overlap for intensity, such as pain or heat. Fuerte also means physically strong; intenso does not usually describe muscular strength.

sections.title: Short
sections.text: Bajo describes low height, including a short person. Corto describes short length or duration; pequeño describes small size more generally.

sections.title: Still
sections.text: Todavía and aún overlap for still or yet. Aun without the accent can mean even, including; it is a different use.

sections.title: There
sections.text: Ahí, allí and allá overlap in English as there. Ahí often points to a more immediate or listener-associated place, allí to a more distant specific place, and allá to a less bounded region or direction; usage varies.

sections.title: Approximately
sections.text: Cerca de and alrededor de can express approximation. Without that numerical construction, cerca means nearby and alrededor means around.
examples: There are about a hundred people.

sections.title: Even
sections.text: Incluso, adverbial hasta and aun can mean even. Hasta also means until or as far as; aún with an accent means still or yet.

sections.title: To listen to
sections.text: Escuchar emphasizes listening with attention. Oír also has a listen-to use, so both fit this cue; hearing a sound does not necessarily imply paying attention.

sections.title: To hear
sections.text: Oír is the general verb for hearing. Escuchar is also used for perceiving a sound, especially in American usage; attention is a useful tendency, not an absolute acceptance boundary.

sections.title: To play
sections.text: Jugar is used for games and sports. Playing a musical instrument normally uses tocar; the English verb play covers both.

sections.title: To touch
sections.text: Tocar means touch and also play an instrument. Jugar means play a game or sport; it does not replace tocar for physical touch.

sections.title: To suppose
sections.text: Suponer, imaginar and asumir can mean taking something as true. RAE recognizes this use of asumir; its separate take-on-responsibility sense does not exclude the assumption sense.

sections.title: To bring
sections.text: Traer brings toward a reference point, often the speaker; llevar takes something toward another destination. The viewpoint matters.

sections.title: To bring closer
sections.text: Acercar brings something closer; alejar moves it farther away. Acercarse and alejarse describe the subject approaching or moving away.

sections.title: To move away
sections.text: Alejar increases distance, while acercar reduces it. The reflexive forms describe the subject's own movement.

sections.title: To lift
sections.text: Levantar and alzar lift an object. Subir can also raise or move something upward; its construction depends on the object and destination.

sections.title: To generate
sections.text: Generar and producir overlap for producing energy. Crear is broader creation and is not a substitute in every technical energy context.

sections.title: To observe
sections.text: Observar emphasizes careful observation. Mirar can also describe watching attentively; ver can simply be visual perception.

sections.title: To appear
sections.text: Aparecer and surgir overlap when something comes into view or emerges. Aparecer also means turn up, including after being missing.

sections.title: To arise
sections.text: Surgir emphasizes emergence or arising. Aparecer can also describe something appearing, without specifying how it developed.

sections.title: To die
sections.text: Morir is die; matar is kill. Fallecer is a formal alternative for a person's death, and morirse is a common pronominal form.

sections.title: To kill
sections.text: Matar takes the being killed as its object. Morir describes dying, not causing another's death.

sections.title: To prevent
sections.text: Impedir and evitar overlap for preventing an event. Evitar also means avoid something without preventing it from existing.

sections.title: To avoid
sections.text: Evitar and esquivar overlap in avoiding an obstacle. Impedir means prevent or obstruct; it does not mean going around an obstacle oneself.

sections.title: Use
sections.text: Uso, utilización and empleo overlap for use. Empleo also means employment or a job; those senses are distinct.

sections.title: Century
sections.text: Siglo and centuria mean century. Década is a decade, ten years.

sections.title: Measurement
sections.text: Medida can be a measurement or a measure taken in response to a problem. Medición concerns measuring; it does not replace medida for a policy measure.

sections.title: Writer
sections.text: Escritor and autor overlap for a writer of literary works. Autor also names the creator of a nonwritten work or the perpetrator of an act.

sections.title: Author
sections.text: Autor and escritor overlap for a book's writer. Autor also applies to other creators; escritor specifically concerns writing.

sections.title: Fact
sections.text: Hecho can be a fact, event or deed. Acto is an act; it does not replace hecho in the selected fact sense.

sections.title: Space
sections.text: Espacio can refer to physical space or a span of time. Período names a time interval, not physical distance between objects.

sections.title: To like
sections.text: Gustar uses the liked thing as its subject and the person as an indirect object. Querer means want or love and uses a different construction.

sections.title: Society
sections.text: Sociedad can name society broadly or an association/company. Comunidad is a community; these related concepts are not identical in every context.

sections.title: Sense
sections.text: Sentido can mean a faculty of perception or a direction. Sensación is a sensation, not the faculty itself.

sections.title: Village; town
sections.text: Pueblo and población can name a settlement. Población also means population; nación is a nation rather than necessarily one settlement.

sections.title: Population
sections.text: Población names the population or a settlement. Pueblo can name a settlement or a people; population size is expressed with población.

sections.title: Voice
sections.text: Voz can be a voice or a lexical item. Término can mean a word or term, but not the sound of a speaking voice.

sections.title: Truth
sections.text: Verdad is truth. Hecho can be an individual fact; the concepts overlap but are not interchangeable in every expression.

sections.title: To seat
sections.text: Sentar seats someone; sentarse means sit down. Sentar bases can mean establish foundations, but establecer does not mean seat a person.

sections.title: Resource
sections.text: Recurso and medio overlap for a means. Recurso also means a legal appeal, a separate sense.

sections.title: Experience
sections.text: Experiencia and práctica overlap for experience gained through doing. Una experiencia can also be an individual event someone lived through.

sections.title: Young person
sections.text: Joven can be a young person of any gender. Muchacho generally means a boy or young man; it is not an exact match for an unrestricted person prompt.

sections.title: Production
sections.text: Producción is production, the process or output. Producto is an individual product; process and item should not be confused.

sections.title: Product
sections.text: Producto names a product. Producción describes producing or its output as a whole.

sections.title: Police officer
sections.text: Policía names the police or an officer. Agente can also mean an officer when the context is police, but has broader meanings.

sections.title: Agent
sections.text: Agente can be a representative or a police officer. Policía fits the officer sense, not every kind of agent.

sections.title: War
sections.text: Guerra is war. Conflicto and lucha are broader and can be nonmilitary; related words need not express the same scale or kind of confrontation.

sections.title: Lesson; class
sections.text: Clase can be a lesson, class or kind. Género and tipo overlap only with its kind/category sense.

sections.title: Morning
sections.text: As a noun, mañana is morning. As an adverb, mañana means tomorrow; the separate cards retain their parts of speech.

sections.title: Afternoon
sections.text: Tarde names the afternoon or early evening, with boundaries varying by place and season. Noche is night; adverbial tarde means late.

sections.title: Awareness
sections.text: Conciencia can be awareness or conscience. Conocimiento overlaps with knowing or awareness, not moral conscience.

sections.title: Knowledge
sections.text: Conocimiento is knowledge. Conciencia can express awareness or conscience, not all accumulated knowledge.

sections.title: Alone
sections.text: Adjectival solo means alone or sole and agrees with its noun. Solamente and adverbial solo mean only; they do not express being without company.
